Exfiltration detection lab: manual test walkthrough

A step-by-step play-through for the owner, to judge what the automated tester can't: whether each hint gets a stuck student moving, whether the sheet reads well, and whether the lab fits a teaching week. The tester (exfil_lab_test.py) has already run every step below on this build and seen each quoted reply. Allow 60 to 90 minutes; each attack that breaks in takes a minute or two.

On the desktop VM you have three pages, served by the hackerbot_server:

  • Hackerbot's chat: http://hackerbot:8080/
  • this walkthrough: http://hackerbot:8080/manual_test.html (copy buttons; ticks are saved in the browser)
  • the lab sheet as students will see it: http://hackerbot:8080/lab_sheet.html

Read each section of the lab sheet before its attacks: the walkthrough checks the sheet as well as the bot. Run everything below in one terminal on the desktop, so the values you type stay set. The password for every prompt is tiaspbiqe2r.

Setup

The IP addresses are in the VM list (or run ip a on each VM).

U=$(whoami); echo "You are $U"
read -p "ids_monitor IP: " IDS
read -p "web_server IP: " WEB
ssh-keygen -q -t ed25519 -N "" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 <<< y >/dev/null 2>&1
ssh-copy-id -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new $U@$IDS
ssh-copy-id -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new $U@$WEB
ids() { ssh -t $U@$IDS "$@"; }
web() { ssh -t $U@$WEB "$@"; }
restart_snort() { ids "sudo service snort stop; sudo service snort start; sleep 5; pgrep -x snort >/dev/null && echo SNORT UP || echo SNORT DOWN"; }
setrules() { printf '%s\n' "$@" | ssh $U@$IDS "cat > /tmp/r; sudo cp /tmp/r /etc/snort/rules/local.rules"; restart_snort; }

The key setup only saves typing passwords for SSH; sudo still asks once per command. setrules replaces local.rules with the rules you give it (one per argument) and restarts Snort, so each step below states the whole rule set.

  • Hackerbot answers hello and list (9 attacks)

Lab sheet: Getting started to Getting Snort up and running

ids "sudo grep -E '^output' /etc/snort/snort.conf; grep -E '^DEBIAN_SNORT_(INTERFACE|HOME_NET)' /etc/snort/snort.debian.conf"
restart_snort
  • Expect: output alert_fast and output log_tcpdump: tcpdump.log; ens19 and "any"; SNORT UP.
  • the "Getting started" section no longer mentions promiscuous mode, and reads fine without it

Lab sheet: Testing your rules

NI=$(web "head -1 ~/trade_secrets/clients.csv" | grep -oE 'QQ[0-9]{6}[A-D]'); echo "First NI number: $NI"
setrules "alert tcp any any -> any any (msg:\"selftest\"; content:\"$NI\"; sid:1000900; rev:1;)"
curl --noproxy '*' ftp://$U:tiaspbiqe2r@$WEB/trade_secrets/clients.csv | head -2
sleep 3; ids "sudo grep selftest /var/log/snort/alert | tail -2"
  • Expect: two CSV lines from curl, then an alert line containing selftest.
  • the sheet's FTP step is clear (and the --noproxy note makes sense)

Attack 1: text-based rule

Say goto 1 and read the alert message in the prompt.

read -p "attack 1 alert message: " M1

Mistake 1, no rule with that message: setrules "", then say ready.

  • Expect: Couldn't find an alert rule with the message
  • hint clear?

Mistake 2, a rule that never matches:

setrules "alert tcp any any -> any any (msg:\"$M1\"; content:\"no-such-text\"; sid:1000001; rev:1;)"

Say ready. Expect: Your rule wasn't triggered.

  • hint clear? (would a student know to test with the FTP step?)

Mistake 3, Snort stopped: ids "sudo service snort stop", then say ready.

  • Expect (before and after the attack): Snort isn't running on the IDS server. Start it with: sudo service snort start.
  • hint clear?

Correct:

R1="alert tcp any any -> any any (msg:\"$M1\"; content:\"$NI\"; sid:1000001; rev:1;)"
setrules "$R1"

Say ready. Expect: Well done! and a flag, then attack 2's prompt.

If the first attack after boot says the connection was too slow to get the data out this time, say ready again: that is the slow-shell case the bot now reports instead of blaming the rule.

  • seen the slow-shell message at any point? (note which attack)

Attack 2: regular expression rule, and the quiz

read -p "attack 2 alert message: " M2
NAME=$(web "head -1 ~/trade_secrets/clients.csv" | cut -d, -f1); echo "First name: $NAME"

Mistake 1, a pcre that contains a name:

setrules "$R1" "alert tcp any any -> any any (msg:\"$M2\"; pcre:\"/$NAME/\"; sid:1000002; rev:1;)"

Say ready. Expect: Your rule contains some of the sensitive data itself.

  • hint clear?

Mistake 2, no pcre:

setrules "$R1" "alert tcp any any -> any any (msg:\"$M2\"; content:\"QQ\"; sid:1000002; rev:1;)"

Say ready. Expect: doesn't use *regular expression* (pcre) matching.

  • hint clear?

Correct (matches the NI number format in either file):

R2="alert tcp any any -> any any (msg:\"$M2\"; pcre:\"/QQ[0-9]{6}[A-D]/\"; sid:1000002; rev:1;)"
setrules "$R1" "$R2"

Say ready (try it twice: Hackerbot picks the real or the fake file at random). Expect: Well done!, a flag and the quiz question.

Quiz: first answer /tmp. Expect: Incorrect (/tmp). Then find the file as a student would, following the sheet's hint:

web "grep -rlE 'QQ[0-9]{6}[A-D]' /tmp 2>/dev/null"
  • Expect exactly one file. answer with its path. Expect: Correct and a flag.
  • the sheet's SSH and grep hints are enough to find it
  • the question is unambiguous (only one copy of the real file in /tmp)

Attack 3: hash-based rule

read -p "attack 3 alert message: " M3
H=$(web "cat ~/trade_secrets/clients.csv" | tail -c +$(( ${#NAME} + 1 )) | head -c 20 | md5sum | cut -d' ' -f1); echo "md5 of the 20 bytes after the name: $H"
PC="content:\"$NAME\"; protected_content:\"$H\"; hash:md5; distance:0; length:20;"

Mistake, protected_content plus an NI number:

setrules "$R1" "$R2" "alert tcp any any -> any any (msg:\"$M3\"; $PC content:\"$NI\"; sid:1000003; rev:1;)"

Say ready. Expect: Your rule contains some of the sensitive data itself.

Correct (name anchor, as the sheet's hint describes):

setrules "$R1" "$R2" "alert tcp any any -> any any (msg:\"$M3\"; $PC sid:1000003; rev:1;)"

Say ready. Expect: Well done! and a flag.

  • the sheet's hint (anchor on a name, distance) is enough to write this rule without the recipe above
  • is it fair that a name is allowed as the anchor but card/NI/phone numbers and emails are not?

Attacks 4 to 8: the incident

Read the sheet's "Incident response" section first. Start a capture:

ids "sudo -v; sudo rm -f /tmp/incident.pcap; sudo nohup tcpdump -i ens19 -w /tmp/incident.pcap >/dev/null 2>&1 &"

Say goto 4, then ready. Expect, after the attack: Got what I came for. Now, investigate: which destination port did the stolen data go to? Then stop the capture and look at it as a student would (Wireshark on the ids_monitor console works too):

ids "sudo pkill -INT -x tcpdump"
HB=$(getent hosts hackerbot | cut -d' ' -f1)
ids "sudo tcpdump -nn -A -r /tmp/incident.pcap 'src host $WEB and dst host $HB'" | grep -oE "> $HB\.[0-9]+:|QQ[0-9]{6}[A-D]" | sort | uniq -c
ids "sudo tcpdump -nn -r /tmp/incident.pcap 'dst host $WEB and dst port 3632'" | head -3

The first command lists the destination port(s) the data went to and each NI number seen (one per record stolen); the second shows the connection to distcc's port 3632 just before.

Attack Wrong answer first Then Expect
4 answer 4444 the port from the capture Incorrect (4444), then a flag
5 one more than the number of records the number of records Incorrect, then a flag
6 answer ssh answer distcc Incorrect (ssh), then a flag
7 answer T1048 answer T1041 Incorrect (T1048), then a flag
8 answer 24 answer 72 Incorrect (24), then a flag
  • the sheet gives enough to answer 4 and 5 from a capture (Conversations, Follow TCP Stream)
  • 6 is answerable from the capture (or too easy, since earlier labs used distcc?)
  • 7 and 8: the sheet points to the right places (ATT&CK Exfiltration tactic, ICO guidance) without giving the answer
  • question-only attacks (5 to 8) are clear: you can answer straight away, ready repeats the question

Attack 9: containment

Read the sheet's IPS and "Containment with a packet filter" sections. Say goto 9.

Mistake 1, no filter: say ready. Expect: I still got a shell on web_server and took the data.

Mistake 2, blocking the website too:

web "sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 3632 -j DROP; sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j DROP"

Say ready. Expect: your website on web_server isn't answering either.

Mistake 3, blocking SSH from the hackerbot_server:

web "sudo iptables -F; sudo iptables -A INPUT -s $HB -p tcp --dport 22 -j DROP"

Say ready. Expect: Couldn't reach the web server and over SSH.

Correct, block the way in (distcc) only:

web "sudo iptables -F; sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 3632 -j DROP; sudo iptables -L INPUT -n --line-numbers"

Say ready. Expect: I couldn't get a shell this time., then Contained: no shell, no data, and the website still works. and a flag, then the IPS question. answer alert (expect Incorrect (alert)), then answer drop (expect a flag).

  • each hint names the problem
  • the sheet's iptables commands are enough to work out the right rule (inbound 3632, or outbound to the hackerbot_server)
  • the IPS page answers the final question

Optional: try blocking the way out instead (web "sudo iptables -F; sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -d $HB -j DROP", or narrower). Which variants pass? Note any that should pass but don't.

Whole lab

  • 11 flags in total
  • the lab fits one teaching week (note your time)
  • the new sheet sections (Testing your rules, Incident response, IPS, Containment) read well
  • anything a student would stop and ask about

Cleanup

web "sudo iptables -F"
setrules ""
